Header:
Date: 2026-03-04

Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Lunaris Head of ML), Oliver Park (Lunaris Infra), Sophie Chen (Product)
Recording ID: ff-20260304-lunaris-23-rec

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
- Reviewed POC cost/economics: tokens/sec/$, batching, caching.
- Redwood shared preliminary cache benchmark showing ~35-50% effective token savings on prefix-heavy workload.
- Discussed tradeoffs between aggressive batching for cost vs tail latency.
- Agreed next steps: run full KV-cache benchmark, update pricing sheet, security deep-dive scheduling.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ava from Redwood, and with me is Dan Kim, our performance SE. How are you all doing?
[00:08] Maya Singh: Good morning, thanks. Lots to cover on cost today, excited to see the numbers.
[00:12] Daniel Kim: Morning Maya, hi Sophie, Oliver. We'll jump into the token economics and then share the cache/batching slides.
[00:20] Oliver Park: Quick note, we've got infra constraints — our traffic spikes at 9am and 3pm PST, so tail latency matters.
[00:27] Sophie Chen: And product wants to keep L1 responses under 350ms if possible.

[00:35] Daniel Kim: Okay, right — we'll surface tradeoffs. First, reminder of test harness: 3M tokens/day simulation, mix of short (50-70 tokens) and long (300-600) prompts, 20% repeat prefixes for caching. The numbers below are from last week's run.
[00:55] Ava Martinez: I'll drop the pricing sheet link in chat — https://redwood.app/sheets/lunaris-poc-pricing (note: internal link).

[01:10] Daniel Kim: Benchmark summary: hosted small cluster (g4-like profile) with quantized 16-bit model variant. Raw throughput measured ~1,200 tokens/sec across the pool without caching, cost estimate ~$0.045 per 1k tokens. With our prefix KV-cache enabled and a ~40% observed cache hit-rate, effective tokens charged dropped by 38%, so tokens/sec/$ improved to roughly 1,900 tokens/sec-equivalent per dollar.
[01:42] Maya Singh: Wait, 38% effective? That seems optimistic — how's hit-rate being calculated? We saw a lower hit-rate in our telemetry.
[01:51] Daniel Kim: Good question. The hit-rate there is on the synthetic workload we provided — about 20% of requests share prefixes, but prefix length is long so more tokens saved per hit. I can share the raw logs. There's a split between prefix-only and KV reuse.
[02:05] Oliver Park: On our side we saw 22% hit by request count; but because the repeated prefixes were large, token-level savings were closer to 33%. So that matches Daniel's number roughly.

[02:20] Ava Martinez: Important for unit-econ is tokens/sec per dollar not just hit-rate. So we model both per-token cost and throughput improvements due to batching. If you batch aggressively you can push tokens/sec up but then tail latency suffers.
[02:36] Sophie Chen: Can you show an example of latency vs batching tradeoff?

[02:42] Daniel Kim: Sure — slide coming, but quick numbers: with batch size targeting 32, average latency for short prompts was ~420ms and p95 ~740ms. With batch size 8, avg ~220ms and p95 ~360ms. Throughput at batch 32 was 2.1k tokens/sec, batch 8 was 1.1k tokens/sec. So cost per effective token halves roughly with big batches but not meet your 350ms p95 SLA.
[03:12] Maya Singh: So product wanting <350ms L1 responses rules out large-batch steady-state unless we use smarter routing?
[03:20] Daniel Kim: Exactly — a hybrid policy helps. Route latency-sensitive routes to low-batch nodes (dedicated smaller pools) and background or lower-priority routes to high-batch pools. Smart routing can preserve user SLAs and still get cost wins on non-critical traffic.

[03:36] Oliver Park: That leads to infrastructure questions — is that handled in Redwood Dedicated or can hosted policy do that?
[03:42] Ava Martinez: Both can. Hosted API supports policy-based routing (latency tiering, region, or cost tier). Dedicated gives more control and predictable throughput but is committed capacity. For Lunaris, if you need strict p95 SLAs during spikes, Dedicated with burst capacity is an option.
[03:58] Maya Singh: Pricing-wise, how does that change the unit-econ? Dedicated has committed cost, so maybe worse on small usage.
[04:05] Ava Martinez: Yup, committed monthly drives lower per-token compute cost but adds fixed commitment. In our cost model we show a break-even point at ~2.8M tokens/day for your workload with 30% caching. Below that hosted is usually cheaper; above that dedicated becomes attractive. I'll send the exact calc.
[04:22] Sophie Chen: Can you explain how KV cache savings show up in billing — are they billed tokens or RPCs?
[04:28] Daniel Kim: Good point — KV-cache reduces compute tokens because the model doesn't re-evaluate prefix tokens. Billing in our hosted model charges generated + non-cached input tokens; cache hits are not billed back to compute, though we still account for small metadata overhead. We put that in the pricing sheet.
[04:45] Maya Singh: There's also the question of correctness — with cache we risk stale KVs if we roll models or change prompt templates. How do you handle cache invalidation?
[04:53] Daniel Kim: We have explicit cache versioning on model rollouts. In rollout you can invalidate prefixes or keep them if compatible. We recommend conservative invalidation for template changes. We'll include our cache invalidation best-practices doc.
[05:10] Oliver Park: Security — we need to confirm that cached values in Dedicated can be encrypted with our KMS, and audit logs exist.
[05:18] Ava Martinez: Yes — for Dedicated and Private we support customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and add audit logs. We'll open a security deep-dive to show exact flows.
[05:30] [00:05:30] Maya Singh: (interrupting) Also curious about cold-start behavior — if caching is empty after deploy, how quickly does hit-rate ramp?
[05:37] Daniel Kim: It depends on request overlap. For production workloads with repeating queries it ramps within hours to days. For highly diverse queries it may remain low. In your traffic we saw a steady-state hit-rate after ~8 hours.
[05:50] Ava Martinez: We'll attach the time-series in the follow-up.

[06:00] [00:06:00] Daniel Kim: Now quick demo of a micro-benchmark I ran: (background typing sounds) — okay, here are the raw numbers — I've uploaded logs: https://redwood.app/bench/lunaris-kv-20260304 (internal). Key numbers: baseline cost $0.045/1k tokens, effective cost w/cache $0.028/1k tokens, throughput improvement ~1.6x.
[06:25] Sophie Chen: Those are promising. What assumptions are baked in re quantization and model variant?
[06:30] Daniel Kim: This test used an int8 quantized variant with attention optimizations; quality diff vs fp16 is minimal for your eval set (we ran BLEU/ROUGE-ish comparisons, will share). For safety-critical prompts we'd use fp16 by default unless customers accept slight quality delta.
[06:46] Maya Singh: Could you run the same with your standard fp16 variant so we can compare?
[06:50] Daniel Kim: Yep — that's on the docket for the next run.

[07:00] [00:07:00] Oliver Park: On networking: we need to confirm egress cost assumptions. Your cost model seems compute-heavy — are we missing cloud egress in our region?
[07:10] Ava Martinez: We accounted for egress where relevant; in Dedicated you control region and we can co-locate to minimize egress. We'll highlight egress assumptions in the sheet.

[07:20] Sophie Chen: Quick question on failover: if the high-batch pool is overloaded, what's fallback?
[07:25] Daniel Kim: Fallback options: auto fallback to a lower-batch compatible variant (lower tokens/sec but lower latency) or route to a warm spare pool. We can set policies per route.

[07:35] Maya Singh: Let's talk about next steps and what we need from Lunaris to validate these models.

[07:40] Ava Martinez: From Redwood: updated pricing sheet with break-even calc, benchmark logs, cache time-series, and a run with fp16 variant. From Lunaris: two production prompt sets, a week (or sample) of traffic trace, and confirmation on latency p95 SLAs.

[07:56] Oliver Park: I'll extract and share a 48-hour traffic trace by Monday.

[08:00] Sophie Chen: Product will pick two prompt sets and share by end of week.

[08:10] Daniel Kim: We'll also run a targeted KV-cache stress test to estimate cold-start ramp and eviction behavior — will include hit-rate per prefix length.

[08:20] Maya Singh: Can you also show a model of batch sizing policy — i.e., how to set thresholds so that class A queries always go low-batch?

[08:27] Ava Martinez: Yes we'll include a sample policy config and suggested thresholds based on your p95 and cost targets.

[08:36] [00:08:36] Ava Martinez: Recap of open items — I'm going to read these out: 1) Ava send pricing sheet and updated unit-econ with break-even point (due 2026-03-06). 2) Daniel run fp16 + int8 comparative run and KV-cache extended logs (due 2026-03-09). 3) Oliver send traffic trace (due 2026-03-09). 4) Sophie/Maya provide prompt sets (due 2026-03-08). 5) Schedule security deep-dive (tentative week of 2026-03-16).
[09:10] Maya Singh: Sounds good. One last question — do you have any quick wins for cost now we can toggle in hosted without infra changes?

[09:18] Daniel Kim: Two quick wins: enable prefix caching for repeatable flows and set a modest batching target for non-latency-critical routes (batch size 12). Both are config flags in hosted and can be enabled with minimal risk.

[09:30] Ava Martinez: I'll note those in the follow-up.

[09:35] Sophie Chen: Great, thanks everyone.

[09:38] Ava Martinez: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the materials.

[09:41] [00:09:41] Meeting ends.
